description: >
  The definitions behind the data model: direction, loops and parallel
  edges, weights, modes, relations and layers, signs, time, space, ego

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Most of the words in network analysis mean more than one thing. A
"bipartite" network is a declared pairing of two node sets to one
person and a graph with no odd cycle to another; a "weight" is a cost to
one program and a strength to the next; "multiplex" means several
relations in the social-network literature and parallel edges in the
`network` package. Programs rarely say which meaning they use, and the
teaching texts an analyst learns from do not always agree with the
software they teach. knappnet fixes one meaning for each term, records it
here, and builds the data model around it.

This article goes through the concepts in the order an analyst meets
them. For each it gives the definition knappnet uses, how a netframe
represents it (which columns and roles in the node and edge tables, and
which S3 class), how [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/), [statnet](https://statnet.org/)'s `network` and networkDynamic,
[tidygraph](https://tidygraph.data-imaginist.com/), [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/), [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home), [Pajek](http://mrvar.fdv.uni-lj.si/pajek/), [ORA](https://www.casos.cs.cmu.edu/projects/ora/), and the teaching
sources differ, and why knappnet chose as it did. The decisions were made
in October 2026 and are recorded, with their alternatives, in
`docs/DECISIONS.md` in the repository. Representations marked *planned*
are decided but not yet implemented; the code in this article builds
plain data frames and shows the decided constructor calls without running
them, so that nothing here depends on functions that do not exist yet.

## A network

**Definition.** A network is a set of nodes and a set of edges, each edge
joining two nodes, together with whatever is known about the nodes, the
edges, and the network as a whole. This is the graph of Wasserman and
Faust (1994, ch. 4) and Newman (2018, ch. 6) with attributes attached;
the smallest network is a dyad (Kadushin 2012).

**In knappnet.** A netframe is two data frames. `nodes` has one row per
node and an identifier column; `edges` has one row per edge and two
endpoint columns. Any other column is an attribute. A list of *roles*
records which columns carry structural meaning (identifier, endpoints,
weight, mode, relation, times, geometry), and a `directed` flag and a
named list `graph` of network-level metadata complete the object.

```{r}
nodes <- data.frame(name = c("ana", "ben", "cy", "dee"),
                    age  = c(31, 45, 28, 52))
edges <- data.frame(source = c("ana", "ana", "ben", "cy"),
                    target = c("ben", "cy",  "cy",  "dee"),
                    years  = c(4, 2, 7, 1))
edges
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Decided constructor call (the endpoint column names are always given
# explicitly or taken from the defaults "source" and "target"; nothing is
# guessed from column positions).
g <- net_frame(edges, nodes, directed = FALSE,
              source = "source", target = "target", id = "name",
              weight = "years", weight_type = "strength")
```

The endpoint columns are named by the `source` and `target` arguments,
whose defaults are the column names `"source"` and `"target"`. Nothing is
guessed from column position, and a table whose endpoints are called
`from`/`to` or `sender`/`receiver` (the names used by Rawlings et al.
2023 and by Shafie and Schoch 2026) is passed with
`source = "sender", target = "receiver"`. Nodes that appear only in the
edge table are added to `nodes` with a message. Every measure returns a
vector aligned with the rows of `nodes` (or of `edges`), so results are
stored as columns.

The constructor validates in four groups, modelled on the checks of
`as.network.data.frame()` in the `network` package (Butts 2008): the
structure (endpoint columns of one atomic type, no missing endpoints,
every endpoint in the node table, unique identifiers), the declared
properties (a declared absence of loops or parallel edges, or a
between-modes-only rule, lists the rows that violate it, and contradictory
declarations are errors rather than silent overrides), attribute sanity
(weights numeric and finite, spells ordered and inside node spells,
geometries in one coordinate reference system), and advisory notes (nodes
added from edges, isolates, identifiers that look 0-based, loops and
parallel edges when none were declared), which `quiet = TRUE` silences.
This validation lives in the engine so that the planned Python package
applies exactly the same rules.

**Other tools.** [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/) (Csardi and Nepusz 2006), `network` (Butts 2008),
[NetworkX](https://networkx.org/) (Hagberg, Schult, and Swart 2008), and [graph-tool](https://graph-tool.skewed.de/) keep attributes
inside an opaque object reached through accessors (`V(g)$x`, `%v%`,
`G.nodes[n]`, property maps); [tidygraph](https://tidygraph.data-imaginist.com/) (Pedersen 2017) and sfnetworks
(van der Meer et al. 2026) expose a node tibble and an edge tibble, which
is the model knappnet shares. [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home) works on matrices with attributes in
separate datasets; [Pajek](http://mrvar.fdv.uni-lj.si/pajek/) stores a network, its partitions, and its vectors
in separate files; [ORA](https://www.casos.cs.cmu.edu/projects/ora/) stores typed node classes and the networks between
them in one meta-network (Tsvetovat, Reminga, and Carley 2004). Every
teaching source consulted builds from an edge list plus a node table
(Rawlings et al. 2023 call the columns sender and receiver and pass the
node table as `vertices`; Almeida-Silva 2024 and Wiederstein 2021 do the
same with igraph), which is the two-table model with other column names.

**Why.** Attributes in data frames need no accessor vocabulary and work
with every data tool the analyst already uses; two of the books spend a
section explaining why a node table must always be supplied so that
isolates and node order survive, which the netframe makes the default.

## Nodes and edges

**Definition.** A node (vertex, actor) is a unit; an edge (tie, link,
line, arc) joins two nodes. Wasserman and Faust (1994, ch. 2) distinguish
structural variables (ties) from composition variables (actor
attributes). knappnet uses *node* and *edge* in code and documentation;
*actor* and *tie* appear when a source uses them.

**In knappnet.** One row per node, one row per edge. A node identifier may
be character, factor, integer, double, logical, or a classed vector such
as a `Date`; it is a label, never a position, and never required to be
1 to *n*. Two edges are two rows even when they join the same nodes
(see parallel edges below).

**Other tools.** [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/) and [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/) number nodes from 1 and 0 respectively
and keep names as an attribute; `network` numbers from 1 and keeps
`vertex.names`; [Pajek](http://mrvar.fdv.uni-lj.si/pajek/) files number vertices and carry labels; [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home) uses
row and column labels. Two teaching sources show readers subtracting 1 or
indexing by row position to satisfy a tool.

**Why.** Identifiers are data. Positions are an implementation detail the
engine handles (0-based, internally) and the analyst never sees.

## Node, edge, and network attributes

**Definition.** A node attribute holds one value per node; an edge
attribute one value per edge; a network attribute describes the whole
network (title, source, collection date, design notes) and has no
structural effect.

**In knappnet.** Node and edge attributes are the non-role columns of
`nodes` and `edges`, of any R type, including list columns and sf
geometry. Network attributes live in `graph`, a named list. Structural
declarations (`directed`, the roles, the mode rule) are fields of the
object and are *not* network attributes.

**Other tools.** `network` stores its structural flags (`directed`,
`loops`, `multiple`, `bipartite`, `hyper`) as network attributes next to
the user's metadata (Butts 2008); [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/) and [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/) keep graph
attributes apart from structure; [Pajek](http://mrvar.fdv.uni-lj.si/pajek/) has one numeric value per line and
separate partition and vector files; [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home) DL and DyNetML carry one value
per cell or link. Conversions therefore write only the weight column to
those single-value formats.

**Why.** Separating structure from metadata means a converter can map
`network`'s flags onto netframe fields and pass the rest through
untouched, and no user attribute can accidentally change how a measure
runs.

## Directed and undirected networks

**Definition.** Direction is a property of the network, not of individual
edges. In a directed network an edge is an ordered pair (source, target):
the edge from `a` to `b` is not the edge from `b` to `a`, and both may
exist. In an undirected network an edge is an unordered pair, and
(`a`, `b`) and (`b`, `a`) denote the same edge. knappnet has no mixed
networks containing both arcs and edges (Wasserman and Faust 1994, ch. 4;
Newman 2018, ch. 6).

**In knappnet.** The `directed` flag. In undirected networks the endpoint
columns are kept exactly as given and never swapped; algorithms treat the
pair as unordered, and the columns round-trip through conversion and
files unchanged.

**Other tools.** [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/), `network`, [tidygraph](https://tidygraph.data-imaginist.com/), [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/) (`Graph` versus
`DiGraph`), [graph-tool](https://graph-tool.skewed.de/), and [NetworKit](https://networkit.github.io/) all use a network-level flag. [Pajek](http://mrvar.fdv.uni-lj.si/pajek/)
has `*Arcs` and `*Edges` sections and allows both in one file, a mixed
network (Batagelj and Mrvar 2026); knappnet reads such a file as
directed, writes each edge as two arcs, and records `graph$source_mixed = TRUE`. sfnetworks reorders the
endpoints of undirected networks so that `from <= to`; knappnet does not.
[UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home) works on square matrices, symmetric or not, and the `symmetrize`
transform is how analysts move between the two (Borgatti, Everett,
Johnson, and Agneessens 2022, ch. 5).

**Why.** One flag is what every library and every teaching source
assumes. Not reordering endpoints keeps the user's columns their own.

## Self-loops

**Definition.** A self-loop is an edge whose two endpoints are the same
node. Loops are allowed, kept, counted when the network is printed, and
each measure states how it treats them (Newman 2018, ch. 6; Wiederstein
2021 gives the same plain definition).

**In knappnet.** A row with equal endpoints. There is no network-level
flag; the printed card reports the count. Helpers to find and remove
loops are planned.

**Other tools.** [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/), [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/), [graph-tool](https://graph-tool.skewed.de/), and [NetworKit](https://networkit.github.io/) allow loops.
`network` has a `loops` flag that defaults to `FALSE`, so loops are
rejected unless declared. [Pajek](http://mrvar.fdv.uni-lj.si/pajek/) keeps loops and can remove them; [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home)
holds them on the matrix diagonal, which most routines ignore. Newman
(2018) and igraph count an undirected loop twice in degree, UCINET-style
routines once; this is the main source of cross-tool differences in
degree and density and is selectable with `convention` (see the
[conventions](conventions.html) article).

**Why.** Data should never be dropped silently. `network`'s default
becomes an explicit removal step rather than a constructor default.

## Parallel edges and simple networks

**Definition.** Two edges are parallel when they have the same endpoints
(as an ordered pair in a directed network, unordered otherwise) *and the
same values of every edge role that distinguishes edges*: the relation
when the network is multiplex and the time spell when it is temporal. A
network with no loops and no parallel edges is simple; otherwise it is a
multigraph (Newman 2018, ch. 6). knappnet networks are multigraphs by
default.

The role-aware rule is what makes a multiplex network behave sensibly:

```{r}
multiplex <- data.frame(source   = c("ana", "ana", "ana", "ben"),
                        target   = c("ben", "ben", "ben", "cy"),
                        relation = c("friendship", "advice", "advice", "advice"))
multiplex
```

Rows 1 and 2 are not parallel (different relations); rows 2 and 3 are.
The network is simple within `friendship` and has one pair of parallel
edges within `advice`.

**In knappnet.** A repeated structural key among the rows of `edges`. The
printed card reports "parallel edges (within the same relation)". Planned
helpers test simplicity, give each edge's multiplicity, and simplify with
a declared rule for combining attributes (sum for weights by default,
first value otherwise), following the idea of [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/)'s `edge.attr.comb`.

**Other tools.** igraph and [graph-tool](https://graph-tool.skewed.de/) are multigraphs by default;
[NetworkX](https://networkx.org/) needs `MultiGraph`; [NetworKit](https://networkit.github.io/) does not support parallel edges;
`network` needs `multiple = TRUE`, and calls parallel edges "multiplex
edges" (Butts 2008), a usage that collides with the social-network
meaning of multiplex used below. [Pajek](http://mrvar.fdv.uni-lj.si/pajek/) keeps multiple lines and offers a
removal with sum, count, minimum, maximum, or single; [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home) matrices
cannot hold them, so multiplicity becomes a cell value. None of the tools
defines parallelism relative to relations or times. Shafie and Schoch
(2026) and Almeida-Silva (2024) reach for igraph's `simplify()`; the
conventions table in `?conventions` records which measures count parallel
edges and which collapse them.

**Why.** An edge list naturally holds repeated pairs, and collapsing them
at construction loses data. Defining "parallel" relative to roles means a
long multiplex edge table is simple within each relation, which is what
analysts expect, and it keeps "multiplex" for several relations and
"parallel" for repeated pairs.

## Weights, and what they mean

**Definition.** A network is weighted when one numeric edge column is
declared the weight; otherwise it is binary. The weight's meaning is
declared once and is one of two things: a **distance** (cost, length,
latency; larger keeps nodes farther apart) or a **strength** (frequency,
intensity, capacity; larger brings nodes closer). Path-based measures use
the weight as a length under `"distance"` and 1/weight under
`"strength"` (Newman 2001; Opsahl, Agneessens, and Skvoretz 2010);
additive measures such as node strength (Barrat et al. 2004) use the
weight as given either way.

**In knappnet.** The `weight` role plus `weight_type`. `net_frame(weight =
"w")` is an error unless `weight_type` is `"strength"` or `"distance"`:
there is no default meaning. The printed card shows the column, the
meaning, and the range. Missing, `NaN`, and infinite weights are stored,
reported, and refused by every measure until resolved.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
net_frame(edges, weight = "years")                           # error: say what the weights mean
net_frame(edges, weight = "years", weight_type = "strength") # years of acquaintance
net_frame(edges, weight = "minutes", weight_type = "distance")
```

**Other tools.** [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/) and [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/) read an attribute called `weight` by
default and treat it as a length in path functions and as an intensity in
strength, modularity, and community detection, in the same session,
without saying so. [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home) and [Pajek](http://mrvar.fdv.uni-lj.si/pajek/) mostly treat values as strengths,
with per-command options. `network` stores a weight as any edge
attribute. Every teaching source consulted reads weight as strength
(Rawlings et al. 2023; Shafie and Schoch 2026; Wiederstein 2021;
Almeida-Silva 2024, who also note that igraph silently stores a numeric
third column as `weight`); only igraph's path functions read it as a
distance, which is why Rawlings et al. devote a section to closeness
computed with the wrong weight direction before switching to tnet.
Epskamp's qgraph treats weights as correlations, a similarity, with sign
inside the value (Epskamp et al. 2012); see signed networks below.

**Why.** The literature is clear that "weight" means two different things
(Newman 2004; Opsahl, Agneessens, and Skvoretz 2010), and the cost of a
wrong default is an invisible error in every path-based result. Requiring
the declaration once, and printing it, is cheaper than any convention.

## One-mode, two-mode, and k-mode networks; the bipartite property

**Definitions.** A *mode* is a declared, disjoint set of nodes of one
kind: actors, events, organisations. A one-mode network has a single set.
A two-mode (affiliation) network has two declared modes and every edge
joins a node of one to a node of the other (Wasserman and Faust 1994,
ch. 8; Breiger 1974; Borgatti and Everett 1997). A k-mode (multipartite)
network has k declared modes with every edge crossing modes (Fararo and
Doreian 1984 for the tripartite case). A *multimode* network, in [ORA](https://www.casos.cs.cmu.edu/projects/ora/)'s
sense, declares modes but allows edges within a mode.

The *bipartite property* is different: a graph is bipartite when its
nodes can be 2-coloured so that no edge joins two nodes of the same
colour, equivalently when it has no odd cycle (Newman 2018, ch. 6). It is
found by search and needs no declaration. A declared two-mode network is
always bipartite; the converse is false (a path, a tree, or an even cycle
is bipartite without being two-mode), and the 2-colouring is not unique
in a disconnected graph.

**In knappnet.** The `mode` node role: any column with two or more
values (character, factor, integer, or logical), with the order of its
levels recorded so that the first mode gives the rows and the second the
columns of the incidence matrix, and a network-level rule stating whether
edges may only cross modes. A logical `type` column, [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/)'s convention,
is accepted as input and written when converting to igraph. Two tests
with two names are planned: one reports the declared modes (today
`net_is_twomode()`), the other tests 2-colourability and returns the
colouring, stopping with a clear message when the graph is not bipartite.

```{r}
affiliations <- data.frame(source = c("ana", "ana", "ben", "cy"),
                           target = c("club A", "club B", "club A", "club B"))
members <- data.frame(name = c("ana", "ben", "cy", "club A", "club B"),
                      mode = c("person", "person", "person", "club", "club"))
members
```

Two-mode networks default to undirected, as in igraph and `network`, but
may be directed (people to events they attended, events to people they
invited) since the edge table carries direction anyway.

**Other tools.** igraph uses a logical `type` vertex attribute (`FALSE`
first kind, `TRUE` second); its R `is_bipartite()` checks that the
attribute exists, while the C core's `igraph_is_bipartite()` runs the
colouring test. `network` records `bipartite` as the count of first-mode
vertices, which must come first. [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/) has no bipartite class, recommends
a 0/1 `bipartite` node attribute "only as a recommendation", passes node
sets explicitly, and raises `AmbiguousSolution` on disconnected graphs.
[Pajek](http://mrvar.fdv.uni-lj.si/pajek/)'s `*Vertices n n1` header gives the size of the first mode; [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home)
holds a rectangular actor-by-event matrix; ORA types nodes by class
(agent, organization, location, event, ...) and networks by the classes
they join; [RSiena](https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~snijders/siena/) takes a bipartite dependent variable with two node sets.
Shafie and Schoch (2026) use "two-mode" for the concept and "bipartite"
for igraph's function names and warn that the coding of `type` decides
which mode is projected; Rawlings et al. (2023) use the two words
interchangeably. The Noordin Top data shipped with knappnet (Cunningham,
Everton, and Murphy 2016) is a multimode multiplex network: one-mode
relations among agents and two-mode affiliations with organisations,
operations, and training events.

**Why.** No tool separates "declared two modes" from "2-colourable", and
both questions are asked. A `mode` role of any type covers two-mode,
k-mode, and multimode data with one mechanism, and it removes a collision
in the DyNetML reader, which writes an ORA node type into a column called
`type`.

## Multiplex, multilayer, and multilevel networks

**Multiplex.** Several relations (kinds of tie) on one node set; each
edge belongs to exactly one relation, and the same pair may be tied in
several (Wasserman and Faust 1994, ch. 3). Formally an edge-coloured
multigraph, and a special case of a multilayer network with one aspect
and no interlayer edges (Kivelä et al. 2014; Battiston, Nicosia, and
Latora 2014 give its structural measures).

*In knappnet:* the `relation` edge role, a discrete column in one long
edge table, as the Noordin data already has. Parallel edges are detected
within relation. Measures take `relation =` to select or combine
relations, and a planned split helper returns one netframe per relation.
Relation-level attributes may go in `graph$relations`. Conversion writes
an edge attribute for [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/) and `network`, relation numbers for [Pajek](http://mrvar.fdv.uni-lj.si/pajek/),
stacked matrices for [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home) DL, and one `<network>` per relation for
DyNetML.

**Multilayer.** Following Kivelä et al. (2014) and De Domenico et al.
(2013): a set of actors, a set of layers (possibly structured by several
aspects, such as relation by time), node-layers (an actor's presence in a
layer), intralayer edges within a layer, and interlayer edges between
layers. The network is node-aligned when every actor is in every layer.
Mucha et al. (2010) call layers "slices"; knappnet treats the word as a
synonym.

*In knappnet (later, as a separate subclass):* node-layers are rows of
`nodes` with `actor` and `layer` roles, `id` stays unique per row, and an
edge is interlayer when its endpoints' layers differ. A planned
`as_multilayer()` lifts a multiplex network by replicating each actor per
relation and adding coupling edges on request. The alternative of one
row per actor with `layer_from`/`layer_to` on edges was rejected: node
attributes that differ by layer would have no home, and interlayer edges
between different actors would need four endpoint columns.

**Multilevel.** In the sense of Lazega et al. (2008), Wang et al. (2013),
and Lazega and Snijders (2016): two or more node sets at distinct levels
(people and organisations), a within-level network at each level, and a
cross-level affiliation network. This is a multimode network whose
relations are typed by the levels they join.

*In knappnet:* the `mode` role with the level labels, within-mode edges
allowed, and the `relation` role naming within-level and cross-level
ties. No new structure; an [ORA](https://www.casos.cs.cmu.edu/projects/ora/) meta-network maps onto it one-to-one.

**Other tools.** UCINET stacks matrices, with a Multiplex transform that
packs them into one coded matrix (Hanneman and Riddle 2005, ch. 16);
Pajek uses relation numbers; ORA holds several networks between node
classes; igraph, [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/), and [tidygraph](https://tidygraph.data-imaginist.com/) have no concept beyond an edge
attribute by convention; multinet (Magnani, Rossi, and Vega 2021) and
pymnet (Nurmi et al. 2024) use actor-layer vertices as the physics
literature does; Raphtory uses "layer" for what knappnet calls a
relation. Rawlings et al. (2023) handle advice and friendship as two
networks; Borgatti et al. (2022) and Cunningham, Everton, and Murphy
(2016) work relation by relation in the UCINET style.

**Why.** "Multiplex" is kept for several relations, "parallel" for
repeated pairs, "multilayer" for node-layers, and "multilevel" for the
Lazega/Snijders design, each with one representation, so that an analyst
coming from any of the tools above finds the word with its usual meaning
and a glossary entry saying which other tool uses it differently.

## Signed networks

**Definition.** Every edge carries a sign, positive or negative,
optionally with a magnitude (Harary 1953; Cartwright and Harary 1956).
Sign is categorical and distinct from weight: a negative tie is not a
shorter path.

**In knappnet (provisional, adopted from the research recommendation and
to be implemented after the core changes).** A `sign` edge role holding
-1 and +1, the values signnet uses so that objects convert without
recoding (Shafie and Schoch 2026, ch. 7). `weight`, if present, is the
magnitude and stays non-negative. A planned `as_signed(x, sign =
"weight")` splits a signed value column into sign and magnitude, which is
how [Pajek](http://mrvar.fdv.uni-lj.si/pajek/), [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home), and correlation networks (Epskamp et al. 2012) arrive;
export writes `sign * weight` back as the single value. Measures to come
are structural balance, the frustration index, Doreian and Mrvar (1996)
partitioning, and signed degree.

**Other tools.** Pajek and UCINET code the sign in the line value;
[igraph](https://r.igraph.org/), [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/), [tidygraph](https://tidygraph.data-imaginist.com/), and `network` have no concept beyond an
attribute; [ORA](https://www.casos.cs.cmu.edu/projects/ora/) has no sign.

**Why.** Keeping sign and magnitude apart means the positivity checks on
path-based measures are never tripped by a negative tie, a network can be
signed without being weighted, and a correlation network read from
qgraph does not get its negative correlations treated as negative
lengths.

## Temporal and dynamic networks

**Vocabulary.** A *temporal network* is one whose edges (and optionally
nodes) carry times, as instants or intervals, so that the structure is
defined at each moment (Holme and Saramäki 2012; Masuda and Lambiotte
2016). *Dynamic network* is the umbrella term and is used only as a
synonym; dynamics *on* networks (diffusion, epidemics) are processes and
out of scope. A *longitudinal* or *panel* network is the same bounded
node set observed at discrete waves (Snijders, van de Bunt, and Steglich
2010). Both R textbooks teach the split as discrete (panel) versus
continuous (event or spell) data (Rawlings et al. 2023, ch. 3; Shafie
and Schoch 2026, ch. 19-20), and knappnet uses the same words.

For continuous time, knappnet uses the terms of Latapy, Viard, and
Magnien (2018): a *contact sequence* is a set of (source, target, time)
triples; a *link stream* gives each link an interval; a *stream graph*
gives nodes intervals too. Holme and Saramäki (2012) call networks with
edge durations "interval graphs", a term knappnet avoids because in graph
theory an interval graph is the intersection graph of intervals on a line
(Lekkerkerker and Boland 1962), an unrelated object. Casteigts et al.
(2012) give the general time-varying-graph formalism as background.

**In knappnet.** The `start`, `end` or `duration`, `node_start`, and
`node_end` roles, with the time class recorded, on a
`c("temporal_netframe", "netframe")` object. `start` alone is a contact
sequence; `start` and `end` a link stream; node spells make a stream
graph.

| Data | Columns |
|---|---|
| Contact sequence | `source`, `target`, `start` |
| Link stream | `source`, `target`, `start`, `end` (or `duration`) |
| Stream graph | the above, plus `node_start`, `node_end` on `nodes` |
| Panel of waves | `source`, `target`, `start = k`, `end = k + 1` |

Spells are half-open, `[start, end)`: an edge is active at `start` and
not at `end`, so consecutive spells and snapshot boundaries are
unambiguous. An edge with `end == start`, or with no `end`, is an
instantaneous contact. `start = -Inf` and `end = Inf` mean the start or
end was not observed (left and right censoring), as in networkDynamic. A
missing `end` when other edges have one is an error, not "forever". An
edge may be active only while both endpoints are present, [Pajek](http://mrvar.fdv.uni-lj.si/pajek/)'s
consistency rule, and the constructor checks it when node spells are
given.

```{r}
contacts <- data.frame(source = c("ana", "ana", "ben"),
                       target = c("ben", "cy",  "cy"),
                       start  = c(1, 1, 3),
                       end    = c(3, 2, 6))
contacts   # active on [1, 3), [1, 2), [3, 6)
```

**Panels.** Waves are time spells: wave k of a panel is the spell
`[k, k + 1)` in a temporal netframe, so every window, snapshot, and
rolling measure applies to panels unchanged. Planned helpers build the
spells from a list of networks (one per wave, as [RSiena](https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~snijders/siena/), networkDynamic's
`network.list`, and the textbooks supply them) and split them back.

**Node presence and time-varying attributes (planned).** A node is
present during its spell and does not exist for measures outside it, not
merely isolated. A node with several spells, and an attribute whose value
changes over time (networkDynamic's temporally extended attributes;
RSiena's behaviour variables per wave), go in optional long tables
`node_spells` and `edge_spells` (identifier, `start`, `end`, and one
column per time-varying attribute); the main tables keep one row per node
and per edge, so `id` stays unique and results stay aligned.

**Other tools.** networkDynamic (Butts et al. 2026) uses half-open
activity spells with `-Inf`/`Inf` censoring, vertex and edge spells,
toggles, and panel lists; tsna computes temporal paths on them.
Raphtory (Steer et al. 2024) timestamps every update and views the same
data as an event graph or a persistent graph with explicit deletions;
teneto (Thompson, Brantefors, and Fransson 2017) uses (i, j, t) rows or
a three-dimensional array; Pajek writes time intervals on vertices and
lines and has an `*Events` format; RSiena takes arrays of adjacency
matrices over waves with composition change in wave units; [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/),
[NetworkX](https://networkx.org/), and [tidygraph](https://tidygraph.data-imaginist.com/) have none; [ORA](https://www.casos.cs.cmu.edu/projects/ora/) keeps one meta-network per
period. Latapy, Viard, and Magnien (2018) use closed intervals.

**Why.** Half-open spells match networkDynamic, the main R interchange
partner, and make a sequence of windows a partition of time. Coding waves
as unit spells gives one engine path for panels and event data, and the
long-table plan for spells and time-varying attributes keeps the
two-table contract and the alignment of results.

## Spatial and spatio-temporal networks

**Definition.** A spatial network has nodes and/or edges with geometry in
one coordinate reference system; its edges are constrained by space but
its adjacency is still given by the edge table, never inferred from
geometry (Barthélemy 2011; Gastner and Newman 2006). A *planar* graph is
one that can be drawn in the plane without edge crossings, a property of
the structure that needs no coordinates; whether a particular geometry
has crossings is a different, spatial question. Road networks are nearly
but not exactly planar (bridges, tunnels).

**In knappnet.** The `node_geometry`, `edge_geometry`, and `crs` roles,
taken from sf geometry columns, on a `c("spatial_netframe", "netframe")`
object; both tables must share a CRS. A spatio-temporal network combines
the spatial and temporal roles on a
`c("spatiotemporal_netframe", "spatial_netframe", "temporal_netframe",
"netframe")` object: fixed geometries with timed edges and nodes
(Williams and Musolesi 2016). Moving nodes are not represented; a
trajectory would be modelled as node spells with a geometry attribute.
knappnet does not require edge linestrings to end at node points; the
check is available on request. A planarity test (graph) and a crossing
count (geometry) are planned under distinct names.

**Other tools.** sfnetworks (van der Meer et al. 2026) requires POINT
nodes and LINESTRING edges whose ends match node coordinates unless
forced, and one CRS for both tables; [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/) and [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/) hold coordinates
as attributes only (NetworkX has a planarity check); [Pajek](http://mrvar.fdv.uni-lj.si/pajek/) stores drawing
coordinates in the `.net` file; [ORA](https://www.casos.cs.cmu.edu/projects/ora/) has a Location node class. The
[spatial networks](spatial-networks.html) article shows the functions.

**Why.** Connectivity is the authoritative data, and geometry a
description of it; requiring the two to agree at construction would
reject real data (a flight edge drawn as a great circle, a node whose
point is a centroid). "Planar" is used only in its graph-theoretic sense.

## Ego networks

**Definition.** The ego network of a node at order k consists of the node
(ego), every node within k steps of it (the alters), and every edge among
them; removing ego and its ties gives the order-1.5 network of ties among
alters that egocentric surveys collect (Marsden 2002; Everett and
Borgatti 2005). An *egocentric* dataset is a collection of such networks,
one per sampled ego, usually with no ties across egos (Burt 1984; Perry,
Pescosolido, and Borgatti 2018).

**In knappnet.** Extraction from a whole network (today `net_ego()`)
returns an ordinary netframe, with ego included by default. For
egocentric survey data an `ego` role on nodes and edges is planned, so
one netframe holds every ego's network and measures run per ego; the
three-table shape (ego, alter, alter-alter tie) that egor uses and both R
textbooks teach (Rawlings et al. 2023, ch. 6; Shafie and Schoch 2026,
ch. 8) is the planned import and export bridge.

**Other tools.** [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/)'s `make_ego_graph()` and [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/)'s `ego_graph()`
include ego; egor's conversion excludes ego by default, a difference the
help page states; [sna](https://cran.r-project.org/package=sna) has `ego.extract`; [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home) and [ORA](https://www.casos.cs.cmu.edu/projects/ora/) have ego-network
routines, and Borgatti et al. (2022, ch. 8) treat ego measures before
centrality.

## Whole and sampled networks

**Definition.** A complete (whole, sociocentric) network records every
tie among all nodes within a declared boundary; deciding who is inside
it is the boundary specification problem (Marsden 1990). A partial
network is anything else: sampled nodes (random, snowball,
respondent-driven), sampled dyads, fixed-choice instruments, or
egocentric collection (Handcock and Gile 2010). Kadushin (2012) organises
the field around whole versus ego-centred networks; Hanneman and Riddle
(2005, ch. 1) make the same split.

**In knappnet.** Not structural. Design metadata (boundary, sampling,
instrument, fixed-choice limit) is recorded in `graph$design`, which
measures do not read and which reports can print. No tool represents
design, and knappnet does not pretend to compute with it.

## Missing data (provisional)

**Definitions.** An *absent* tie was observed not to exist: no row. A
*missing* tie is a dyad whose status was not observed (non-response,
out-of-range, censoring). A *missing node* is a known node whose own
ties were not observed, a non-respondent, whose incoming ties reported by
others may still be known. A *structural zero* is a dyad that cannot be
tied by design and is excluded from denominators and models; a
*structural one* is fixed as present (Kossinets 2006; Robins, Pattison,
and Woolcock 2004; Wasserman and Faust 1994, ch. 2).

**In knappnet (provisional, after the core changes).** An `na` node role
marks non-respondents, the operational notion in the textbooks (Rawlings
et al. 2023, ch. 4, where a non-respondent's row is entirely `NA` and a
zero in their column does not mean the tie would not have been
reciprocated). An `na` edge role marks dyads whose status is unknown.
Measures stop when any unresolved `na` node or edge exists unless an
`na_action` says what to do (treat as absent, as present, or exclude the
dyad from denominators), mirroring the existing rule that `NA` weights
are stored but refused. Structural zeros and ones are better kept as a
rule or a pair table than as rows, since in edge-list form they are
mostly absent pairs; that representation is still open.

**Other tools.** `network` marks missing edges with an `na` attribute and
returns `NA` from the adjacency matrix for them; [RSiena](https://www.stats.ox.ac.uk/~snijders/siena/) codes `NA` for
missing, 10 for structural zeros, and 11 for structural ones (Ripley et
al. 2026); [UCINET](https://sites.google.com/site/ucinetsoftware/home) has a missing-value code that routines treat
differently; [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/), [NetworkX](https://networkx.org/), [tidygraph](https://tidygraph.data-imaginist.com/), [Pajek](http://mrvar.fdv.uni-lj.si/pajek/), and [ORA](https://www.casos.cs.cmu.edu/projects/ora/) do not
distinguish missing from absent. Borgatti, Carley, and Krackhardt (2006)
and Kossinets (2006) are the standard references on what missingness does
to measures.

## Hypergraphs and simplicial complexes (out of scope)

**Definitions.** A hypergraph is a node set with a family of hyperedges,
each a non-empty subset of nodes of any size; a simplicial complex is a
hypergraph closed under taking subsets (Battiston et al. 2020; Bianconi
2021). Both share the incidence structure of a two-mode network (nodes by
hyperedges) but are not two-mode networks: a hyperedge has no identity
beyond its member set, a duplicate hyperedge means multiplicity, and
simplicial closure is a constraint no two-mode network has (Torres et al.
2021 discuss when each representation is right).

**In knappnet.** Not first-class; an edge has two endpoints. The
documented exchange is a two-mode netframe with `mode = c("node",
"hyperedge")`, and the clique expansion to a weighted one-mode network is
the ordinary two-mode projection:

```{r}
hyperedges <- data.frame(source = c("ana", "ben", "cy", "ana", "dee"),
                         target = c("h1",  "h1",  "h1", "h2",  "h2"))
hyperedges   # h1 = {ana, ben, cy}, h2 = {ana, dee}
```

`network` supports hyperedges with `hyper = TRUE`; XGI (Landry et al.
2023) is the reference library for higher-order data. Measures on
hypergraphs are out of scope until a need appears.

## A glossary of clashes

| knappnet says | Also called | Means something else in |
|---|---|---|
| parallel edges | multi-edges, multiple lines | `network`: "multiplex edges" |
| multiplex (relations) | multirelational, edge-coloured | `network`'s `multiple` flag (parallel edges); Raphtory and graph-tool: "layer" |
| multilayer (node-layers) | multislice (Mucha et al. 2010) | Raphtory: edge colouring |
| multilevel (Lazega/Snijders) | linked design | statistics: hierarchical models; Kivelä et al.: a synonym of multilayer |
| two-mode (declared) | affiliation, bipartite in SNA usage | graph theory: 2-colourable |
| bipartite (property) | 2-colourable, no odd cycle | [igraph](https://r.igraph.org/) R: "has a `type` attribute"; SNA: two-mode |
| link stream, contact sequence | temporal network | Holme and Saramäki: "interval graph", which in graph theory is a different object |
| planar (graph) | | geometry: no crossing linestrings |
| distance weight | cost, length | igraph's `net_strength()`: the same column as an intensity |
| strength weight | intensity, frequency | igraph's `net_distances()`: the same column as a length |
